ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the left side is the input Vin, and the upper input terminal passes through a series resistor labeled 9Ω to reach the right output node; this output node is connected downward to a branch, and the branch is composed of a 1Ω resistor and a 1F capacitor connected in series and then connected to the bottom common line. The output Vo is taken between this output node and the bottom common line. Therefore this is a voltage divider network in which a 9Ω series resistor feeds a parallel load branch, and the load branch impedance is a 1Ω resistor in series with a 1F capacitor. Reasoning: The capacitor impedance is 1/(sC)=1/s, so the shunt branch impedance Z=1+1/s=(s+1)/s. The voltage transfer function is H(s)=Vo/Vin=Z/(9+Z)=((s+1)/s)/(9+(s+1)/s)=(s+1)/(10s+1). Written in standard form, H(s)=(1+s/1)/(1+s/0.1), so the zero frequency is 1 rad/s and the pole frequency is 0.1 rad/s. The maximum phase-lag frequency of this first-order lead/lag network is ωm=sqrt(ωp·ωz)=sqrt(0.1×1)=0.316 rad/s, approximately 0.32 rad/s.

method.method_draft: First describe the image as a voltage divider: series input resistor R1=9 Ω feeding a shunt load made of R2=1 Ω in series with C=1 F, with Vo across the shunt branch. Compute the shunt impedance Z=R2+1/(sC)=1+1/s=(s+1)/s. Then H(s)=Vo/Vin=Z/(9+Z)=((s+1)/s)/(9+(s+1)/s)=(s+1)/(10s+1). Rewrite as H(s)=(1+s/1)/(1+s/0.1), so the zero frequency is 1 rad/s and the pole frequency is 0.1 rad/s. Apply ωm=sqrt(0.1×1)=0.316 rad/s, reported as about 0.32 rad/s.
